en.content:
Calculate the cell EMF in V for

Pt|H2 (1 atm) | HCl (0.01 M) || AgCl(s) | Ag(s) at 298 K

If $\Delta G_f^\circ$ values are at 298 K is -102.6 kJ/mol for AgCl(s) and -126.3 kJ/mol for HCl (aq.).
en.explanation:
The cell is

$$ \text{Pt}|\text{H}_2(1\text{ atm})|\text{HCl}(0.01\text{ M})||\text{AgCl}(s)|\text{Ag}(s) $$

The half-cell reactions are:

At anode:

$$ \text{H}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}^+ + 2e^- $$

At cathode:

$$ \text{AgCl}(s) + e^- \rightarrow \text{Ag}(s) + \text{Cl}^- $$

So the overall cell reaction is:

$$ \text{H}_2(g) + 2\text{AgCl}(s) \rightarrow 2\text{Ag}(s) + 2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{Cl}^- $$

This is the same as writing:

$$ \text{H}_2(g) + 2\text{AgCl}(s) \rightarrow 2\text{Ag}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) $$

Now,

$$ \Delta G^\circ = \sum \Delta G_f^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta G_f^\circ(\text{reactants}) $$

Given:

$$ \Delta G_f^\circ[\text{AgCl}(s)] = -102.6 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} $$

$$ \Delta G_f^\circ[\text{HCl}(aq)] = -126.3 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} $$

For elements like $\text{H}_2$ and $\text{Ag}$,

$$ \Delta G_f^\circ = 0 $$

So,

$$ \Delta G^\circ = 2(-126.3) - 2(-102.6) $$

$$ \Delta G^\circ = -252.6 + 205.2 $$

$$ \Delta G^\circ = -47.4 \text{ kJ} $$

$$ \Delta G^\circ = -47400 \text{ J} $$

Now use :

$$ \Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}} $$

Here, $n = 2$.

$$ E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = \frac{47400}{2 \times 96500} $$

$$ E^\circ_{\text{cell}} \approx 0.246 \text{ V} $$

Now apply the Nernst equation :

$$ E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.0591}{n}\log Q $$

For the reaction,

$$ Q = \frac{[\text{H}^+]^2[\text{Cl}^-]^2}{P_{\text{H}_2}} $$

Since HCl is $0.01$ M and it ionises completely,

$$ [\text{H}^+] = 0.01 = 10^{-2} $$

$$ [\text{Cl}^-] = 0.01 = 10^{-2} $$

Also,

$$ P_{\text{H}_2} = 1 $$

So,

$$ Q = (10^{-2})^2(10^{-2})^2 $$

$$ Q = 10^{-8} $$

Now,

$$ E_{\text{cell}} = 0.246 - \frac{0.0591}{2}\log(10^{-8}) $$

$$ E_{\text{cell}} = 0.246 - \frac{0.0591}{2}(-8) $$

$$ E_{\text{cell}} = 0.246 + 0.236 $$

$$ E_{\text{cell}} \approx 0.482 \text{ V} $$

So,

$$ E_{\text{cell}} \approx 0.48 \text{ V} $$

Correct option: A.

298 K पर Pt|H2 (1 atm) | HCl (0.01 M) || AgCl(s) | Ag(s)

यदि 298 K पर $\Delta G_f^\circ$ के मान AgCl(s) के लिए -102.6 kJ/mol और HCl (aq.) के लिए -126.3 kJ/mol हैं।

en.content: A metal rod is dipped in a solution of its ions. Its electrode potential is independent of
en.explanation:
The electrode potential of a metal dipped in a solution of its own ions depends on:

  • nature of the metal

  • concentration of metal ions in solution

  • temperature

For a metal electrode,

$$ M^{n+} + ne^- \rightleftharpoons M $$

According to the Nernst equation,

$$ E = E^\circ + \frac{RT}{nF}\ln [M^{n+}] $$

This shows that electrode potential depends on temperature $T$ and ion concentration $[M^{n+}]$. The standard electrode potential $E^\circ$ depends on the nature of the metal.

But the area of the metal exposed only affects the rate or amount of current that may flow, not the electrode potential itself.

So, the correct answer is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option C: area of the metal exposed}} $$

hi.content: एक धातु की छड़ को उसके आयनों के विलयन में डुबाया जाता है। इसका इलेक्ट्रोड विभव किससे स्वतंत्र होता है:

en.content:
Given below are two statements.

Statement I $E_{cell}$ and $\Delta G$ of cell reaction both are extensive properties.

Statement II $\Delta G^\circ$ and $K$ are independent of electrode potential.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below.

options.content: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.

en.explanation:
Analysis of Statement I

  • $E_{cell}$ (Cell Potential): Cell potential is an intensive property. It represents the potential difference between two electrodes and does not depend on the amount of substance (or the number of moles) undergoing the reaction. If you multiply a balanced cell reaction by a coefficient, the $E_{cell}$ remains unchanged.

  • $\Delta G$ (Gibbs Free Energy): Gibbs free energy is an extensive property. It depends directly on the amount of substance reacting. This is evident from the relationship:

$$\Delta G = -nFE_{cell}$$

Here, $n$ represents the number of moles of electrons transferred. Since $n$ changes depending on the stoichiometry of the reaction, $\Delta G$ changes accordingly.

Conclusion for Statement I: Since $E_{cell}$ is intensive and $\Delta G$ is extensive, Statement I is incorrect.

Analysis of Statement II

Statement II claims that $\Delta G^\circ$ and $K$ (equilibrium constant) are independent of electrode potential. Let's look at their mathematical relationships with standard cell potential ($E^\circ_{cell}$):

  1. Relation to $\Delta G^\circ$:

$$\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{cell}$$

This equation clearly shows that the standard Gibbs free energy change ($\Delta G^\circ$) is directly dependent on the standard electrode potential ($E^\circ_{cell}$).

  1. Relation to $K$ (Equilibrium Constant):

Using the Nernst equation at equilibrium (where $E_{cell} = 0$):

$$E^\circ_{cell} = \frac{2.303RT}{nF} \log K$$

This equation demonstrates that the equilibrium constant $K$ is also fundamentally dependent on the standard electrode potential.

Conclusion for Statement II: Since both $\Delta G^\circ$ and $K$ depend on the standard electrode potential, Statement II is incorrect.

Option D: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.

कथन II $\Delta G^\circ$ और $K$ इलेक्ट्रोड विभव से स्वतंत्र होते हैं।

en.content:
Calculate the cell potential $E$ at $25^{o}C$ for the reaction

2Al(s) + 3Fe$^{2+}$(aq) → 2Al$^{3+}$(aq) + 3Fe(s)

[Given : [Fe$^{2+}$] = 0.02 M, [Al$^{3+}$] = 0.2 M

$E^{ {o}}_{ {Al}^{3+}/{Al}}$ = -1.65 V, $E^{ {o}}_{ {Fe}^{2+}/ {Fe}}$ = -0.44 V and

$\left( \frac{2.303RT}{F} \right) = 0.06$
en.explanation:
• Cathode (Reduction): $Fe^{2+} / Fe$ ($E^\circ = -0.44\text{ V}$)

  • Anode (Oxidation): $Al^{3+} / Al$ ($E^\circ = -1.65\text{ V}$)

$$E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$$

$$E^\circ_{cell} = -0.44\text{ V} - (-1.65\text{ V}) = 1.21\text{ V}$$

Balance the half-reactions to find the total number of electrons exchanged:

  • Oxidation: $Al \rightarrow Al^{3+} + 3e^-$ (Multiply by 2 $\rightarrow 6e^-$)

  • Reduction: $Fe^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Fe$ (Multiply by 3 $\rightarrow 6e^-$)

Therefore, $n = 6$.

For the given reaction $2Al(s) + 3Fe^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow 2Al^{3+}(aq) + 3Fe(s)$:

$$Q = \frac{[Al^{3+}]^2}{[Fe^{2+}]^3}$$

$$Q = \frac{(0.2)^2}{(0.02)^3} = \frac{0.04}{0.000008} = 5000$$

Using the Nernst equation and the given value $\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.06$:

$$E_{cell} = E^\circ_{cell} - \frac{2.303RT}{nF} \log Q$$

$$E_{cell} = 1.21 - \frac{0.06}{6} \log(5000)$$

Calculate the log term:

$$\log(5000) = \log(5 \times 10^3) = \log(5) + 3 \approx 0.699 + 3 = 3.699$$

$$E_{cell} = 1.21 - 0.01 \times 3.699$$

$$E_{cell} = 1.21 - 0.03699$$

$$E_{cell} \approx 1.173\text{ V}$$

Rounding to two decimal places, the cell potential is +1.17 V.

The correct choice is Option A.

en.content:
Consider the cell,

Ag | AgBr(s) | Br− (aq) || Cl− (aq) | AgCl(s) | Ag(s) at 25°C.

The solubility product constants of AgBr and AgCl are respectively $6 \times 10^{-13}$ and $3 \times 10^{-10}$. For what ratio of the concentrations of Br− and Cl− ions when the emf of the cell is zero? ($E^\circ_{\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}} = 0.08\ \text{V}$)
en.explanation:
For a metal-insoluble salt electrode, the standard reduction potential is directly linked to the solubility product ($K_{sp}$). The standard cell potential for this specific combination of electrodes is given by:

$$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = \frac{RT}{nF}\ln \frac{K_{sp}(\mathrm{AgBr})}{K_{sp}(\mathrm{AgCl})} \quad \dots \text{(i)}$$

  • Anode (Oxidation): $\mathrm{Ag}(s) + \mathrm{Cl}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl}(s) + e^{-}$

  • Cathode (Reduction): $\mathrm{AgBr}(s) + e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag}(s) + \mathrm{Br}^{-}(aq)$

  • Net Cell Reaction: $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}(aq) + \mathrm{AgBr}(s) \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl}(s) + \mathrm{Br}^{-}(aq)$

(Note: The reference simplifies the net reaction conceptually to just the aqueous ions: $\mathrm{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Br}^{-}$)

For the net reaction, the reaction quotient is $Q = \frac{[\mathrm{Br}^{-}]}{[\mathrm{Cl}^{-}]}$. The Nernst equation becomes:

$$E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln \frac{[\mathrm{Br}^{-}]}{[\mathrm{Cl}^{-}]}$$

Since the cell is at equilibrium (the emf is zero), $E_{\text{cell}} = 0$:

$$0 = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln \frac{[\mathrm{Br}^{-}]}{[\mathrm{Cl}^{-}]}$$

$$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = \frac{RT}{nF}\ln \frac{[\mathrm{Br}^{-}]}{[\mathrm{Cl}^{-}]} \quad \dots \text{(ii)}$$

By equating equation (i) and equation (ii), the $\frac{RT}{nF}$ terms cancel out:

$$\frac{[\mathrm{Br}^{-}]}{[\mathrm{Cl}^{-}]} = \frac{K_{sp}(\mathrm{AgBr})}{K_{sp}(\mathrm{AgCl})}$$

  • $K_{sp}(\mathrm{AgBr}) = 6 \times 10^{-13}$

  • $K_{sp}(\mathrm{AgCl}) = 3 \times 10^{-10}$

$$\frac{[\mathrm{Br}^{-}]}{[\mathrm{Cl}^{-}]} = \frac{6 \times 10^{-13}}{3 \times 10^{-10}}$$

$$\frac{[\mathrm{Br}^{-}]}{[\mathrm{Cl}^{-}]} = 2 \times 10^{-3}$$

$$\frac{[\mathrm{Br}^{-}]}{[\mathrm{Cl}^{-}]} = \frac{2}{1000} = \frac{1}{500}$$

en.content: What will be the reduction potential of hydrogen electrode at 298 K which is prepared with the help of aq. solution of acetic acid with 0.01 M conc. at 1 atm pressure? ($K_a = 2.6 \times 10^{-5}$)
en.explanation:
For a weak acid like acetic acid, the concentration of hydrogen ions is given by $[\mathrm{H}^{+}] = \sqrt{K_a \times c}$.

$$[\mathrm{H}^{+}]^2 = K_a \times c$$

$$[\mathrm{H}^{+}]^2 = 2.6 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.01 = 2.6 \times 10^{-7}$$

For the reduction half-reaction: $2\mathrm{H}^{+}(aq) + 2e^{-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_2(g)$

The Nernst equation is:

$$E_{\text{Redn}} = E_{\text{Redn}}^{\circ} - \frac{0.059}{2} \log \frac{P_{\mathrm{H}_2}}{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]^2}$$

Since the standard reduction potential of hydrogen is $E_{\text{Redn}}^{\circ} = 0 \text{ V}$ and $P_{\mathrm{H}_2} = 1 \text{ atm}$:

$$E_{\text{Redn}} = 0 - \frac{0.059}{2} \log \left( \frac{1}{2.6 \times 10^{-7}} \right)$$

$$E_{\text{Redn}} = -\frac{0.059}{2} \log \left( \frac{10^7}{2.6} \right)$$

$$E_{\text{Redn}} = -\frac{0.059}{2} [7 - \log 2.6]$$

Given that $\log 2.6 \approx 0.415$:

$$E_{\text{Redn}} = -\frac{0.059}{2} [7 - 0.415]$$

$$E_{\text{Redn}} = -\frac{0.059}{2} \times 6.585$$

$$E_{\text{Redn}} \approx -0.194 \text{ V}$$

Therefore, the correct choice is Option C.

en.content:
The equilibrium $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} (aq) + \mathrm{Cu}(s) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cu}^+ (aq)$ established at 293 K corresponds to

$\dfrac{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Cu}^+]^2} = 1.010 \times 10^2$.

The standard potential $E_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}}^\circ = 0.33\ \mathrm{V}$ at this temperature.

The value of standard potential of $E_{\mathrm{Cu}^+ / \mathrm{Cu}}^\circ$ will be
en.explanation:
At equilibrium, the cell potential $E_{\text{cell}} = 0$. Using the Nernst equation at $298\text{ K}$ (approximate standard standard state calculation):

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = \frac{0.0591}{n} \log K$$

For the reaction $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(aq) + \mathrm{Cu}(s) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cu}^+(aq)$, the number of exchanged electrons is $n = 1$, and $K = \frac{[\mathrm{Cu}^+]^2}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}$.

We are given $\frac{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Cu}^+]^2} = 1.010 \times 10^2$, which means $K = \frac{1}{1.010 \times 10^2}$.

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = \frac{0.0591}{1} \log \left(\frac{1}{1.010 \times 10^2}\right)$$

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.0591 \times (-2.004) \approx -0.118\ \mathrm{V}$$

The overall cell reaction can be split into two half-reactions:

  • Cathode (Reduction): $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^+$
  • Anode (Oxidation): $\mathrm{Cu} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^+ + e^-$

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}$$

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}^+} - E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^+/\mathrm{Cu}} = -0.118\ \mathrm{V} \qquad \dots \text{(a)}$$

Using the relationship $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$ for the standard reduction potentials:

(i) $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu} \quad (\Delta G_1 = -2FE_1)$

(ii) $\mathrm{Cu}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu} \quad (\Delta G_2 = -1FE_2)$

(iii) $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^+ \quad (\Delta G_3 = -1FE_3)$

Reaction (iii) is obtained by subtracting equation (ii) from equation (i):

$$\Delta G_3 = \Delta G_1 - \Delta G_2$$

$$-1FE_3 = -2FE_1 - (-1FE_2)$$

$$-E_3 = -2E_1 + E_2$$

$$E_3 = 2E_1 - E_2$$

$$E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}^+} = 2 \times (0.33) - E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^+/\mathrm{Cu}}$$

$$E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}^+} = 0.66 - E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^+/\mathrm{Cu}}$$

Substitute this expression back into equation (a):

$$-0.118 = (0.66 - E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^+/\mathrm{Cu}}) - E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^+/\mathrm{Cu}}$$

$$-0.118 = 0.66 - 2E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^+/\mathrm{Cu}}$$

$$2E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^+/\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.66 + 0.118$$

$$2E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^+/\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.778$$

$$E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^+/\mathrm{Cu}} = \frac{0.778}{2} = 0.389\ \mathrm{V}$$

Therefore, the correct choice is Option A.

en.content:
Consider the cell

$\mathrm{H}_2$(Pt) | $\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+$(aq) | | $\mathrm{Ag}^+$ | Ag.

1 atmpH = 5.03$x$ M

The measured EMF of the cell is 1.0 V. What is the value of $x$? $E^0_{\mathrm{Ag}^+ / \mathrm{Ag}} = +0.8$ V. [T = 25°C]
en.explanation:
The given cell representation is:

$$\mathrm{H_2(Pt)\ (1\ atm)\ |\ H_3O^+\ ||\ Ag^+\ (xM)\ |\ Ag}$$

The net cell reaction for a 1-electron transfer is: $\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{H}_2(g) + \mathrm{Ag}^+(aq) \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^+(aq) + \mathrm{Ag}(s)$

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}} = 0.8\ \text{V} - 0.0\ \text{V} = 0.8\ \text{V}$$

Using the Nernst equation (taking the standard approximation of $0.06$ for $\frac{2.303RT}{F}$ to make calculations easier):

$$E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.06}{n} \log \frac{[\mathrm{H}^+]}{[\mathrm{Ag}^+]}$$

Substitute the given values ($E_{\text{cell}} = 1.0\ \text{V}$, $n = 1$, and $[\mathrm{Ag}^+] = x$):

$$1.0 = (0 + 0.8) - \frac{0.06}{1} \log \frac{[\mathrm{H}^+]}{x}$$

$$0.2 = -0.06 \log \frac{[\mathrm{H}^+]}{x}$$

$$-\frac{0.2}{0.06} = \log \frac{[\mathrm{H}^+]}{x}$$

$$-\frac{10}{3} = \log [\mathrm{H}^+] - \log x$$

$$-\frac{10}{3} = -\mathrm{pH} - \log x$$

$$\frac{10}{3} = \mathrm{pH} + \log x$$

We are given $\mathrm{pH} = 5.03$ and $\frac{10}{3} \approx 3.33$:

$$3.33 = 5.03 + \log x$$

$$\log x = 3.33 - 5.03$$

$$\log x = -1.7$$

$$x = 10^{-1.7}$$

This can be rewritten using standard log properties ($\log 2 \approx 0.30$):

$$x = 10^{-2 + 0.3} = 10^{0.3} \times 10^{-2}$$

$$x = 2 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{M}$$

Therefore, the correct choice is Option A.

en.content: The standard emf for the cell reaction Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu is 1.10 volt at 25°C. The emf for the cell reaction when 0.1 M Cu2+ and 0.1 M Zn2+ solutions are used at 25°C is
en.explanation:
For the given cell reaction: $\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+} + \mathrm{Cu}$

The Nernst equation at $25^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is:

$$E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{n} \log \frac{[\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}$$

  • Standard emf ($E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$) = $1.10\ \text{V}$
  • Number of electrons transferred ($n$) = $2$
  • Concentration of product ions, $[\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}]$ = $0.1\ \text{M}$
  • Concentration of reactant ions, $[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]$ = $0.1\ \text{M}$

Substitute the values into the Nernst equation:

$$E_{\text{cell}} = 1.10 - \frac{0.059}{2} \log \left( \frac{0.1}{0.1} \right)$$

$$E_{\text{cell}} = 1.10 - 0.0295 \log(1)$$

Since the logarithm of $1$ is exactly $0$, the entire subtraction term drops out:

$$E_{\text{cell}} = 1.10 - 0 = 1.10\ \text{V}$$

Therefore, the correct choice is Option A.

en.content: The EMF of a concentration cell consisting of two zinc electrodes, one dipping into $\frac{M}{4}$ sol. of zinc sulphate & the other into $\frac{M}{16}$ sol. of the same salt at $25^{\circ} C$ is
en.explanation:
In a concentration cell, both electrodes are made of the same material (Zinc in this case). Therefore, the standard cell potential is zero:

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0\ \text{V}$$

For a concentration cell to act spontaneously (producing a positive EMF), oxidation (anode) must occur at the lower concentration half-cell, and reduction (cathode) must occur at the higher concentration half-cell.

  • Anode ($C_1$, lower concentration): $\frac{M}{16}$
  • Cathode ($C_2$, higher concentration): $\frac{M}{4}$

The number of electrons exchanged in the Zinc half-reaction ($\mathrm{Zn} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Zn}^{2+} + 2e^-$) is $n = 2$.

The Nernst equation for a concentration cell at $25^\circ\mathrm{C}$ simplifies to:

$$E_{\text{cell}} = -\frac{0.0591}{n} \log \frac{C_1}{C_2}$$

Substitute the given values into the equation:

$$E_{\text{cell}} = -\frac{0.0591}{2} \log \left( \frac{1/16}{1/4} \right)$$

$$E_{\text{cell}} = -\frac{0.0591}{2} \log \left( \frac{1}{4} \right)$$

Since $\log(1/4) = \log(4^{-1}) = -\log(4)$:

$$E_{\text{cell}} = \frac{0.0591}{2} \log(4)$$

We know that $\log(4) = \log(2^2) = 2 \log(2)$:

$$E_{\text{cell}} = \frac{0.0591}{2} \times 2 \log(2)$$

$$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.0591 \times \log(2)$$

Taking $\log(2) \approx 0.3010$:

$$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.0591 \times 0.3010$$

$$E_{\text{cell}} \approx 0.0178\ \text{V}$$

Therefore, the correct choice is Option C.

$$ \mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{~s})+\mathrm{Sn}^{2+}(0.002 \mathrm{M}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(0.02 \mathrm{M})+\mathrm{Sn}(\mathrm{~s}) . $$

The Gibb's free energy change for the above reaction at 298 K is $x \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. The value of $x$ is $\_\_\_\_$ .

[Nearest integer]

$$ \begin{aligned} {\left[E_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} / \mathrm{Cu}}^{\circ}=0.34 ; E_{\mathrm{Sn}^{2+} / \mathrm{Sn}}^{\circ}\right.} & =-0.14 \mathrm{~V} ; \mathrm{F} & \left.=96500 \mathrm{C} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right] \end{aligned} $$
en.explanation:
For the given reaction: $\mathrm{Cu(s) + Sn^{2+}(0.002\ M) \rightarrow Cu^{2+}(0.02\ M) + Sn(s)}$

Tin ($\mathrm{Sn}^{2+}$) is reduced (cathode) and Copper ($\mathrm{Cu}$) is oxidized (anode).

$$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}}$$

$$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = -0.14 - (0.34) = -0.48\ \text{V}$$

$$E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{n} \log \frac{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Sn}^{2+}]}$$

Since 2 electrons are exchanged, $n = 2$:

$$E_{\text{cell}} = -0.48 - \frac{0.059}{2} \log \left(\frac{0.02}{0.002}\right)$$

$$E_{\text{cell}} = -0.48 - 0.0295 \log(10)$$

$$E_{\text{cell}} = -0.48 - 0.0295 \approx -0.51\ \text{V}$$

The relationship between free energy and cell potential is:

$$\Delta G = -nF E_{\text{cell}}$$

$$\Delta G = -2 \times 96500 \times (-0.51)$$

$$\Delta G = 98430\ \text{J/mol}$$

Convert to $\text{kJ/mol}$ by dividing by 1000:

$$\Delta G = 98.43\ \text{kJ/mol}$$

Expressing the result in the requested scientific format ($x \times 10^{-2}$):

$$\Delta G = 9843 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{kJ/mol}$$

Therefore, the value of $x$ is 9843.

Given the data at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$,

$$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{Ag}+\mathrm{I}^{-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{AgI}+e^{-} ; \mathrm{E}^0=0.152 \mathrm{~V} \\ & \mathrm{Ag} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ag}^{+}+e^{-}, \mathrm{E}^0=-0.800 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned} $$

The value of $K_{\mathrm{sp}}$ for $A g \mathrm{l}$ is $-x$. The value of $x$ is $\_\_\_\_$.

(Nearest integer)

$$ \left(2.303 \frac{R T}{F}=0.059 \mathrm{~V}\right) $$
en.explanation:
The given reactions are provided as oxidation half-reactions (electrons are lost on the product side):

  • $\mathrm{Ag}(s) + \mathrm{I}^-(aq) \longrightarrow \mathrm{AgI}(s) + e^-\ \ \ \ (E^\circ_1 = 0.152\ \text{V})$
  • $\mathrm{Ag}(s) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ag}^+(aq) + e^-\ \ \ \ (E^\circ_2 = -0.800\ \text{V})$

The solubility product ($K_{sp}$) represents the equilibrium of the sparingly soluble salt dissolving into its ions:

$$\mathrm{AgI}(s) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Ag}^+(aq) + \mathrm{I}^-(aq)$$

To obtain this net reaction, we need to reverse the first reaction (making it a reduction) and add it to the second reaction (which remains an oxidation):

  • Cathode (Reduction): $\mathrm{AgI}(s) + e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ag}(s) + \mathrm{I}^-(aq)$
    (Since the reaction is reversed, its potential changes sign: $E^\circ_{\text{red}} = -0.152\ \text{V}$)
  • Anode (Oxidation): $\mathrm{Ag}(s) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ag}^+(aq) + e^-$
    ($E^\circ_{\text{ox}} = -0.800\ \text{V}$)

The standard cell potential ($E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$) for the net reaction is the sum of the oxidation and reduction potentials:

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{red}} + E^\circ_{\text{ox}}$$

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = -0.152\ \text{V} + (-0.800\ \text{V}) = -0.952\ \text{V}$$

The relationship between the standard cell potential and the equilibrium constant ($K_{sp}$) is given by:

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = \frac{0.059}{n} \log K_{sp}$$

Since exactly $1$ mole of electrons is exchanged in the balanced net reaction, $n = 1$:

$$-0.952 = \frac{0.059}{1} \log K_{sp}$$

$$\log K_{sp} = \frac{-0.952}{0.059}$$

$$\log K_{sp} = -16.135$$

The standard convention in such problems equates $\log K_{sp}$ to $-x$ (or $K_{sp} = 10^{-x}$). By comparing our result:

$$-x = -16.135$$

$$x = 16.135$$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we get $16$.

Therefore, the value of $x$ is 16.

en.content: The cell; $\mathrm{Zn}\left|\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(1 \mathrm{M}) \| \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(1 \mathrm{M})\right| \mathrm{Cu}\left(E_{\text {cell }}^{\circ}=1.10 \mathrm{~V}\right)$ was allowed to be completely discharged at 298 K . The relative concentration of $\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}$ to $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\left(\frac{\left[\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\right]}\right)$ is $10^x$. The value of $x$ is $\_\_\_\_$ (Nearest integer)
en.explanation:
When a galvanic cell is completely discharged, it means the redox reaction has reached equilibrium. At this state, the cell can no longer do useful work, and the cell potential ($E_{\text{cell}}$) becomes zero.

$$E_{\text{cell}} = 0$$

For the given cell $\mathrm{Zn}|\mathrm{Zn}^{2+} || \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}|\mathrm{Cu}$, the net cell reaction is:

$$\mathrm{Zn}(s) + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(aq) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + \mathrm{Cu}(s)$$

The number of electrons exchanged in this process is $n = 2$.

At equilibrium, the reaction quotient becomes the equilibrium constant ($K_c$):

$$K_c = \frac{[\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}$$

The Nernst equation at $298\text{ K}$ is given by:

$$E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{n} \log K_c$$

Substituting $E_{\text{cell}} = 0$:

$$0 = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{2} \log \left(\frac{[\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}\right)$$

$$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = \frac{0.059}{2} \log \left(\frac{[\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}\right)$$

We are given $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 1.10\ \text{V}$ and $\frac{[\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]} = 10^x$:

$$1.10 = \frac{0.059}{2} \log(10^x)$$

Using the property of logarithms ($\log 10^x = x$):

$$1.10 = 0.0295 \times x$$

$$x = \frac{1.10}{0.0295}$$

$$x = 37.288$$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we get $37$.

Therefore, the value of $x$ is 37.

The hydrogen electrode is dipped in a solution of $\mathrm{pH}=4$ at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The potential of the electrode will be $\ldots \ldots \ldots \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{V}$

$\left(\frac{2.303 R T}{F}=0.009 \mathrm{~V}\right)$ (Nearest integer)
en.explanation:
$$2\mathrm{H}^+(aq) + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_2(g)$$

$$E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{2} \log \frac{P_{\mathrm{H}_2}}{[\mathrm{H}^+]^2}$$

We know that $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 0\ \mathrm{V}$, $P_{\mathrm{H}_2} = 1\ \mathrm{bar}$, and $[\mathrm{H}^+] = 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{M}$ (since $\mathrm{pH} = 4$).

$$E_{\text{cell}} = 0 - 0.059 \times (-4)$$

$$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.236\ \mathrm{V}$$

$$0.236\ \mathrm{V} = 23.6 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{V}$$

Rounding $23.6$ to the nearest integer, we get $24$.

Therefore, the value to fill in the blank is 24.

en.content: For the $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} \mid \mathrm{Cu}$ electrode, the standard reduction potential is +0.34 V. Given that the solubility product of $\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{OH})_2$ is $1.0 \times 10^{-19}$, find the pH of the solution when the reduction potential of this electrode is 0.31 V. $(2.303 R T / F=0.06)$
en.explanation:
For the reduction half-reaction: $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu}(s)$

The Nernst equation at the given temperature is:

$$E = E^\circ - \frac{2.303RT}{nF} \log \frac{1}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}$$

We are given $E = 0.31\ \text{V}$, $E^\circ = 0.34\ \text{V}$, $n = 2$ (since 2 electrons are exchanged), and $\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.06$:

$$0.31 = 0.34 - \frac{0.06}{2} \log \frac{1}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}$$

$$-0.03 = -0.03 \log \frac{1}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}$$

$$1 = \log \frac{1}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}$$

$$\frac{1}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]} = 10^1 = 10$$

$$[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}] = \frac{1}{10} = 0.1\ \text{M} = 10^{-1}\ \text{M}$$

The dissociation of copper(II) hydroxide is:

$$\mathrm{Cu(OH)_2}(s) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(aq) + 2\mathrm{OH}^-(aq)$$

The solubility product expression is:

$$K_{sp} = [\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}][\mathrm{OH}^-]^2$$

$$1.0 \times 10^{-19} = (10^{-1}) \times [\mathrm{OH}^-]^2$$

$$[\mathrm{OH}^-]^2 = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{-19}}{10^{-1}} = 10^{-18}$$

$$[\mathrm{OH}^-] = 10^{-9}\ \text{M}$$

First, find the pOH:

$$\mathrm{pOH} = -\log[\mathrm{OH}^-] = -\log(10^{-9}) = 9$$

Assuming standard temperature conditions where $\mathrm{pH} + \mathrm{pOH} = 14$:

$$\mathrm{pH} = 14 - \mathrm{pOH}$$

$$\mathrm{pH} = 14 - 9 = 5$$

Therefore, the pH of the solution is 5.

hi.content: $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} \mid \mathrm{Cu}$ इलेक्ट्रोड के लिए, मानक अपचयन विभव +0.34 V है। दिया गया है कि $\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{OH})_2$ का विलेयता गुणनफल $1.0 \times 10^{-19}$ है, जब इस इलेक्ट्रोड का अपचयन विभव 0.31 V हो, तो विलयन का pH ज्ञात कीजिए। $(2.303 R T / F=0.06)$
